title: Seneca Consoles His Mother from Exile
text:
In 41 AD the emperor Claudius exiled the philosopher Seneca to the island of Corsica on a charge of adultery with the emperor's niece. Seneca was in his forties, at the height of his career. His mother, Helvia, was left in Rome, and he knew the news had struck her hard.

So, around 42, Seneca did something unusual: he wrote a consolation to his mother for his own misfortune. He began by admitting that he had hesitated, since a man still suffering should not try to heal another. Then he reminded her of all she had already endured. Her own mother had died giving birth to her. She had lost an uncle she loved and her husband. Less than twenty days after Seneca's own young son died in her arms, she heard that Seneca had been exiled.

Exile, he argued, was only a change of place. Nature had given every human being the same sky, and a mind that was sound could be at home anywhere. He was not unhappy, he assured her, and asked her not to grieve for him. He pointed her toward the comforts she still had: his brothers, her grandchildren, her devoted sister. Above all, he urged her to turn to philosophy, and regretted that his father's old-fashioned strictness had not allowed her to study more deeply.

Seneca remained in Corsica for eight years. He was recalled in 49 to become tutor to the young Nero.
lesson: Sometimes the best way to comfort a worried parent is to show them how we are bearing up. Care can flow from child to parent too.
source: Seneca, To Helvia on Consolation (Ad Helviam Matrem de Consolatione), Dialogues 12
